title: A/B Routing: Fetch One Variant and Preserve the Assignment
prompt: Fetch an API containing variant URLs, choose one uniformly, and return that page. Preserve the choice in a cookie. For deterministic practice, variants are [A,B], new clients draw U=[0.1,0.8,0.49] in [0,1), and the first client returns with cookie A. Which pages are fetched?
approach: Parse the nonempty list. Without a valid assignment, choose index floor(U*k) for k URLs.
Fetch only the selected page. Store its stable variant identifier in a cookie and reuse it while valid.
Each index occupies an interval of length 1/k. Uniform sampling does not guarantee equal short-run counts.
complexity: O(B) parsing/storage for B URL-list bytes; one selected-page fetch. Stream the page.
pitfalls: Treat removed or invalid cookie values as unassigned.
followUp: What if the variant list changes?
answer: The new clients fetch [A,B,A]. The returning first client fetches A without another random draw.
sourceNote: Historical public hiring assignment; this trace covers routing and cookie persistence, not its full deployment task.

title: Ping Accounting: Match Replies and Exclude Duplicates
sourceTitle: Cloudflare 2020 internship application: systems ping assignment
prompt: Build ping accounting for probes 1,2,3 sent at 0,10,20 ms. Replies are (1,8),(3,35),(1,40),(2,90). Accept only the first matching reply arriving less than 50 ms after sending. Report at 100 ms.
approach: Record unique probe identities and monotonic send times; reject replies not matching this run.
Ignore duplicates and expired replies. For each accepted reply, RTT=receive_time-send_time.
At the cutoff, loss=(sent-accepted)/sent. Compute RTT statistics from accepted replies only.
complexity: Expected O(S+R) bookkeeping and O(S) storage for S sends and R replies.
pitfalls: Counting duplicates can produce negative loss.
No accepted replies means RTT statistics are undefined.
followUp: How would you prevent an old reply matching a reused sequence number?
answer: Two replies count: RTTs 8 and 15 ms; mean 11.5 ms; loss 1/3.
sourceNote: Historical hiring task: implement an ICMP ping CLI. Fixed events, deadlines, and late-reply policy are teaching assumptions, not network measurements.

title: Horseplay: Enumerate Legal Knight Moves
sourceTitle: LinkedIn Learning C++ Code Challenges: Challenge 6, Horseplay
prompt: Given a valid chess square from a1 through h8, return all squares reachable by one knight move. Ignore other pieces. Sort the result lexicographically for this exercise.
approach: Decode file and rank as coordinates in [0,7].
Generate offsets (±1,±2) and (±2,±1), covering all eight moves.
Keep coordinates inside the board, encode them as squares, and sort. Every legal move has exactly one generated offset.
complexity: O(1) time and auxiliary space on a fixed 8-by-8 board; at most eight outputs.
pitfalls: A knight can jump over intervening pieces.
Reject destinations outside the board before encoding them.
followUp: How would BFS find the fewest moves between two squares when some destinations are blocked?
answer: From a1 the destinations are [b3,c2]; from d4 there are eight.
sourceNote: Official educational practice published by LinkedIn Learning; not evidence of a LinkedIn hiring question. Output sorting is a local convention.

examples.explanation: All eight offsets remain inside the board.
The opposite corner also has two legal moves.

title: IPv4 Validation: Parse Every Octet Completely
sourceTitle: LinkedIn Learning C++ Code Challenges: Challenge 8, IP Address Validation
prompt: Validate dotted-decimal IPv4 text: exactly four nonempty ASCII digit fields, each 0..255. For this exercise, forbid whitespace, signs, and leading zeros except the field 0. Consume the entire input.
approach: Scan characters and delimiters while tracking field count, length, first digit, and numeric value.
Require one to three digits, value 0..255, and the leading-zero rule.
Accept only after validating the final field and counting exactly four fields. A valid numeric prefix is insufficient.
complexity: O(n) time for n input characters with O(1) auxiliary state; valid inputs have at most 15 characters.
pitfalls: A trailing dot creates an empty field.
Permissive integer conversion may accept signs or ignore trailing text.
followUp: Why does IPv6 require a different grammar?
answer: 192.0.2.7 is valid; 01.2.3.4 and 256.2.3.4 are invalid under these rules.
sourceNote: Official educational practice, not a LinkedIn interview claim. The source specifies decimal fields 0..255; strict syntax and leading-zero rules are explicit local assumptions.

examples.explanation: All four fields satisfy the rules.

title: Finding Relatives: Stop at the First Repeated Surname
sourceTitle: LinkedIn Learning C++ Code Challenges: Challenge 11, Finding Relatives
prompt: Read comma-separated GivenName Surname records, with one space per record. Compare surnames case-sensitively. Scan left to right; at the first repeated surname, return its earliest full name and the current name. Otherwise return null.
approach: Parse in input order; the first completed duplicate wins.
Maintain a hash map from each surname to its first full name. Check for an existing entry before inserting.
The map retains each surname's earliest name, so the first successful lookup gives the required pair.
complexity: Expected O(B) time and O(B) storage for B input characters using string hashing; output may occur before EOF.
pitfalls: A shared surname is not proof of kinship.
General CSV needs quoting rules beyond this restricted grammar.
followUp: What is the output cost of returning every matching pair?
answer: Ava Chen,Bo Diaz,Cy Chen,Di Diaz returns [Ava Chen,Cy Chen].
sourceNote: Official educational practice, not LinkedIn hiring evidence. Ordering, case sensitivity, and null results are explicit exercise conventions.

title: Game of Life: Update a Wrapping Grid Simultaneously
sourceTitle: LinkedIn Learning C++ Code Challenges: Challenge 13, Conway's Game of Life
prompt: Compute one simultaneous generation on a wrapping 10-by-10 grid. A live cell survives with two or three live neighbors; a dead cell becomes live with exactly three. Input/output lists contain live [row,column] cells; sort outputs lexicographically.
approach: For every cell, count its eight neighbors in the old grid.
Wrap each neighbor coordinate as (coordinate+offset+10) mod 10, avoiding negative remainders.
Write results into a second grid, then swap. Read only old states when counting.
complexity: O(HW) time and O(HW) auxiliary space per H-by-W generation.
pitfalls: Updating cells immediately changes later neighbor counts.
Wrapping differs from permanently dead borders.
followUp: How can two bits per cell retain old and new states in one grid?
sourceNote: Official LinkedIn Learning educational practice, not a LinkedIn hiring question. The public prompt specifies the wrapping board; examples are original.
